## The ask

Do the 990 data show any patterns in nonprofit locations and finances in the
Nashville metro, in connection with recent survey work on the Tennessee
nonprofit workforce? Exploratory only, five hours, no committed product.
(Requester specifics are in the gitignored `_private.md`.)

## Geography

"Nashville metro" is OMB CBSA 34980, Nashville-Davidson--Murfreesboro--Franklin,
TN: 14 counties (Davidson, Williamson, Rutherford, Sumner, Wilson, Maury,
Robertson, Dickson, Cheatham, Hickman, Macon, Smith, Cannon, Trousdale), 2023
delineation, held fixed across years. Geography is composed by joining the
published `county-fips` and `cbsa` crosswalks onto the geocoded Unified BMF.
"Davidson" is Metro Nashville; "collar" means the other 13 counties.

## Data and method

- **Registered universe:** geocoded Unified BMF (rolling, read 2026-10-12),
  one row per EIN with `first_year_in_bmf` / `last_year_in_bmf`. County
  resolution is 100% for Tennessee organizations active in 2026.
- **Finances and workforce:** e-file v2.1 Form 990 Part I and Part IX tables,
  TY2012-2023, one return per EIN x tax year (amended and group returns keep
  the latest timestamp). Tax year and return type are taken per row. Full
  Form 990 only: 990-EZ and 990-PF carry no employee or compensation lines.
  Employees = Part I line 5 (a headcount, including part-time). Pay per
  employee = Part IX lines 5-10 (all compensation, benefits, payroll tax)
  divided by employees, kept when between $5,000 and $400,000.
- **Government grants:** NCCS e-file Phase 0 `government_grants` (Form 990
  Part VIII line 1e), vintage v2026.06, TY2020-2023. A blank line is treated
  as zero everywhere.
- **Main population:** 501(c)(3) public charities excluding hospitals and
  universities (NTEE v2 subsectors HOS and UNI), so a handful of health
  systems, electric cooperatives and employee benefit trusts do not drive
  the totals. The all-organizations view is in the exploration scripts.
- **Benchmarks:** 19 peer metros (Memphis, Knoxville, Austin, Charlotte,
  Raleigh, Indianapolis, Louisville, Columbus, Kansas City, Jacksonville,
  Oklahoma City, Atlanta, Denver, St. Louis, Cincinnati, Richmond,
  Birmingham, San Antonio, Phoenix), the rest of Tennessee, and the rest of
  the US. Dollars are CPI-U adjusted to 2023. Population from Census county
  estimates (vintages 2019 and 2023); private-sector pay from BLS QCEW.

### Caveats to read before citing

1. TY2023 is about 5% short of complete in this e-file release (filer counts
   dip from 2022 to 2023 everywhere). 2019 to 2022 comparisons are given
   where they change the picture.
2. Location is the filing address. Organizations headquartered in Davidson
   (Second Harvest, United Way, community action agencies) serve the region,
   so per-resident spending by county overstates how concentrated services are.
3. Leaving the full-990 panel can mean closure, merger, falling under the
   $200,000 gross-receipts threshold (switching to 990-EZ), or late filing.
4. Employee counts on the 990 are headcounts with no hours, so pay per
   employee tracks the wage bill per head, not a wage rate.
5. Pre-2021 e-file years cover only organizations that e-filed voluntarily.
   Series start at TY2012 by house rule.

## Findings

### 1. Population moved to the collar counties; nonprofit infrastructure did not

Davidson's share of the metro's registered nonprofits has fallen steadily
(47% in 2000, 42% in 2026) as the collar grew, but the money and the jobs
remain in Davidson and, to a lesser degree, Williamson.

Registered 501(c)(3) organizations per 10,000 residents:

| County | Pop. 2023 | Pop. growth 2010-23 | Orgs/10k 2010 | Orgs/10k 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 712,334 | 13% | 49.4 | 58.2 |
| Williamson | 264,460 | 44% | 56.5 | 62.6 |
| Rutherford | 367,101 | 39% | 24.1 | 29.2 |
| Sumner | 207,994 | 29% | 26.9 | 34.5 |
| Wilson | 163,674 | 43% | 28.6 | 34.6 |
| Maury | 110,760 | 36% | 33.0 | 38.4 |

Full-990 charity spending and jobs per resident (excluding hospitals and
universities), 2023:

| County | Charity filers | Expenses per resident | Charity employees per 1,000 residents | Human services expenses per resident | Human services employees per 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 883 | $6,546 | 67.1 | $1,564 | 21.0 |
| Williamson | 331 | $2,994 | 25.7 | $992 | 9.1 |
| Rutherford | 145 | $1,008 | 17.1 | $272 | 2.6 |
| Wilson | 74 | $840 | 7.6 | $104 | 1.3 |
| Sumner | 115 | $441 | 5.1 | $195 | 2.2 |
| Maury | 57 | $1,070 | 12.5 | $176 | 2.9 |

Rutherford is the second most populous county in the metro and has grown
39% since 2010, yet it hosts 37 human-services charities filing a full 990
with 2.6 employees per 1,000 residents, against 21 in Davidson. Williamson,
the wealthiest county, is the exception: it is as dense in organizations as
Davidson. Every county's organization density rose between 2010 and 2023, so
the collar is catching up in counts, but not in capacity.

### 2. Nashville's charities run on private money, not government money

Government grants (Form 990 line 1e) as a share of total revenue, 2023,
charities excluding hospitals and universities:

| | Share reporting any government grants | Government grants / revenue (aggregate) | Share of charities 25%+ government funded |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nashville metro | 30% | 12.7% | 16% |
| Rest of Tennessee | 39% | 18.2% | 23% |
| Rest of US | 33% | 15.3% | 18% |
| Nashville human services | 34% | 13.2% | 19% |
| US human services | 38% | 23.5% | 23% |

Nashville ranks 10th of 20 peer metros on aggregate government share, but
the gap is widest in human services, where the metro's charities draw 13
cents of revenue from government against 24 cents nationally. Within the
metro the split is sharp: Davidson charities get 14.8% of revenue from
government, Williamson 3.6%, Rutherford 4.9%. Among human-services
charities, Davidson is at 15.7% and the collar at 7.8%.

The flip side shows in the revenue mix. The median Nashville charity gets
79% of revenue from contributions and grants of all kinds (US: 69%), and
that share jumped in 2020 (72% to 82%) and has not come back down. The
largest government recipients are charter school networks (KIPP, LEAD,
Valor, RePublic, STEM Prep, each 84 to 96% government funded), the
Tennessee Performing Arts Center, the Mid-Cumberland community action and
human resource agencies, and Second Harvest.

### 3. More organizations, more spending, no more jobs

Charities excluding hospitals and universities, 2019 to 2023 (real 2023 $):

| | Full-990 filers | Employees | Real expenses | Median real pay per employee |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nashville metro | +26% | -4% | +7% | +9.9% |
| Rest of Tennessee | +23% | -13% | -26% | -0.8% |
| Rest of US | +16% | +1% | +2% | +0.7% |

Nashville added full-990 charities faster than any peer metro except
Jacksonville and Indianapolis, and its real spending grew while the rest of
Tennessee's shrank. Headcount did not follow: 65,500 employees in 2023
against 68,600 in 2019 (2022: 68,500, so the 2023 dip is partly caveat 1).
Human services went from 386 to 514 filers while employees slipped from
21,900 to 20,000.

### 4. Pay rose faster than anywhere in the peer set, mostly because low-paying organizations dropped out

The median Nashville charity's real pay per employee rose from $39,800 to
$43,700 (+9.9%), the largest gain among the 20 metros. Human services rose
from $36,400 to $41,700 (+15%). For comparison, BLS private-sector average
pay in Davidson rose 6% in real terms over the same years, and private
social-assistance pay (NAICS 624) rose 12%, from $31,000 to $41,500. So
nonprofit human-services pay kept pace with the local private market for
the same work, which is not what most peers managed.

But the gain is largely compositional. Among organizations present in both
2019 and 2023, Nashville's median within-organization real pay change was
+4.1%, barely above the US figure of +3.5%. The difference is who left:

| Nashville charities with staff in 2019 | n | Median real pay per employee, 2019 |
|---|---|---|
| Still filing a full 990 in 2023 | 753 | $41,560 |
| No longer filing a full 990 in 2023 | 128 | $31,629 |

Elsewhere in the country the leavers paid the same as the stayers ($37,800
vs $37,700). In Nashville the organizations that closed, merged, or shrank
below the 990 threshold paid a quarter less than those that survived. That
is consistent with the survey finding that Tennessee nonprofits were more
optimistic about hiring: the ones still standing are the ones that could
pay.

### 5. Human services: holding staff, losing margin

Among human-services charities present in both 2019 and 2023, the share
ending the year in deficit rose from 34% to 43% (US: 40% to 44%), while the
median organization's reserves stayed near 11 months of spending. Nashville
started from a better position and ended at the national level. Across all
Nashville charities, deficits are at 37% (US 41%) and 19% hold under three
months of net assets (US 21%): not a sector in distress, but one that spent
its 2020-2021 cushion. Volunteers reported by Nashville charities fell from
300,000 in 2019 to 275,000 in 2023 and the median organization's volunteer
count dropped from 50 to 34.

## What this could become

- A county-level "capacity map" for Metro and the Community Foundation:
  Finding 1 as a map with human-services capacity per resident, which is
  where their service-area questions live. Needs the service-area caveat
  made explicit, ideally by checking a few regional organizations' Schedule
  O descriptions.
- A funding-mix brief: Finding 2 is new relative to the survey work and
  speaks directly to a community foundation and a city government deciding
  who fills what gaps. TY2024 Phase 0 data (partial) could extend it.
- The pay and exit pattern in Finding 4 deserves a closer look before it is
  cited: which 128 organizations left, and whether they closed or just
  switched to the 990-EZ.

## Reproducibility

Scripts in this folder run in order: `build-panel.R`, `build-peers.R`,
`explore-1-universe.R` through `explore-7-govgrants.R`. All reads are
pinned in `_pins.csv`. The national e-file tables are the TY2012-2023 files
synced for `requests/2026-06-milwaukee-msa` (sha256 in that folder's
`_efile_inputs.csv`). Population and QCEW inputs are fetched from Census
and BLS public URLs (see `explore-5-charities.R` and `_private.md`).
